content2.content: Imagine a user is filling out a long form in your app. They get a phone call, switch to another app, and after a while, the operating system, needing more memory, terminates your app's process in the background. When the user returns, will they find their form data gone, forcing them to start over? With State Restoration, you can prevent this frustrating experience.

content3.content: This article covers how to save and restore your app's UI state, ensuring a seamless user experience even when the OS terminates your app.

content5.content: What is State Restoration and Why is it Important?

content6.content: State Restoration is the process of saving the UI state of your app before it's killed by the operating system and restoring it when the user returns.

content7.content:
On Android: The Android OS can kill background app processes at any time to reclaim memory for foreground apps. This is known as "process death."
On iOS: While less frequent, iOS can also terminate background apps under memory pressure. More commonly, iOS state restoration ensures a seamless feel when multitasking.

content8.content: Without state restoration, the user loses their place. They lose scroll positions, text entered into fields, selected tabs, and progress through a multi-step flow. Implementing state restoration makes your app feel robust and reliable.

content9.content: Core Concepts of Flutter's Restoration Framework

content10.content: Flutter provides a built-in framework to handle this, centered around a few key concepts:

content11.content:
RestorationMixin: A mixin that you add to your State class. It provides the necessary methods and functionality to participate in state restoration.
RestorableProperty: A special class that wraps a piece of state you want to save (like an int, String, or bool). It knows how to save and restore its own value. Flutter has many built-in subclasses like RestorableInt, RestorableString, RestorableTextEditingController, etc.
RestorationBucket: Think of this as a key-value store for your restoration data. The framework provides a "bucket" to your widget where it can store its RestorablePropertys.
RestorationScope: A widget that enables state restoration for a part of the widget tree. You typically wrap your entire app with it.
restorationId: A unique string ID you give to a widget that has state to restore. This ID is used as the key in the RestorationBucket to find the saved data.

content12.content: Implementing State Restoration in Your Flutter App

content15.content: Let's modify a simple counter app to support state restoration.

content16.content: Step 1: Wrap Your App with RestorationScope

content17.content: In your main.dart, wrap your MaterialApp (or CupertinoApp) with a RestorationScope.

content19.content: Step 2: Use the RestorationMixin in Your StatefulWidget

content20.content: In the State class of the widget whose state you want to save, add with RestorationMixin.

content22.content: Step 3: Use RestorableProperty for Your State

content23.content: Instead of using a standard type like int, use its restorable counterpart.

content26.content: The RestorationMixin requires you to override two things:

content28.content:
A getter for restorationId: This provides a unique ID for this widget within its current scope.
The restoreState method: This is where you register all your RestorablePropertys with the framework.

content29.content: That's it! With these changes, the counter's value will be saved and restored.

content32.content:
Run your app on an Android emulator or device.
Enable "Don't keep activities" in the Developer Options on the device. This makes the OS more aggressive about killing background processes.
Increment the counter in your app.
Press the home button to send the app to the background.
Open another app (like Chrome or Settings) to ensure your app's process is killed.
Return to your app from the recent apps list.
If state restoration is working, the counter will reappear with its previous value, not zero. On iOS, you can simulate this by stopping the app from your IDE while it's running and then re-launching it.

content34.content: The goal is to restore the user's state of interaction with the UI, not all of your application's data.

content36.content:
The text in TextFields (RestorableTextEditingController).
Scroll positions of long lists (RestorationMixin on the State of a ScrollView).
The index of a currently selected tab.
Whether a checkbox or switch is active.
Progress through a multi-page form or wizard.

content38.content:
Application State: User authentication tokens, user profile data, or data fetched from an API. This should be managed by your global state management solution (Provider, Riverpod, etc.) and should be re-fetched or loaded from a persistent cache when the app starts.
Animation State: It's usually better to restart animations.
Anything that depends on a live network connection.

content40.content: State restoration is a key feature of a professional, high-quality Flutter application. It shows users that you respect their time and effort by preserving their context, even when the underlying operating system is working against you. By using Flutter's built-in restoration framework with RestorationMixin and RestorableProperty, you can easily add this powerful feature to your app, significantly improving the user experience.
